I believe it is not an extreme statement when I say that if we had the surpluses earned by the fire and life insurance companies of Canada since confederation with the accumulated interest they would pay off the national debt. When we come to fire insurance it is more easy to determine the actual profits, because at the end of [DOT] the year, when the policies run out and the losses are paid, anything that is left over is direct profit, outside of expenses of course. I find that in the year 1919 the amount of fire insurance placed in Canada was $4,923,000,000; the amount of premiums received $40,000,000; and the losses $16,679,000; leaving a net surplus in the hands of the companies of $23,352,000. This appears to be just an average year, because in the next year, 1920, I find the amount of fire insurance placed in Canada was $5,969,000,000; the premiums received amounted to over $50,000,000; and the losses paid $21,000,000; leaving a surplus in the hands of the company of nearly $29,000,000. Therefore it seems to me the government should take this matter into very serious consideration, and I certainly see no justification for the government placing itself in the humiliating position of coaxing these private companies to remove this discrimination against our Canadian ports.
* When we come to consider the question of rates, the greatest discrimination, or the greatest difference between pre-war rates and after-war rates seems to be in the cattle rates. We find that whereas before the war cattle were handled from Montreal to Liverpool at from $6 to $7.30 per head, at present we are paying at from $20 to $25 per head. I must say I am not very hopeful we will ever be able to build up any very large live cattle trade with Great Britain under the present circumstances. I believe that if we are ever to develop a large live cattle trade with England it will be done through the Hudson Bay route. I know that many hon. members do not agree with that statement, but those of us who have been devoting months of time and study to the consideration of the reports and information in connection with Hudson bay are firmly convinced of the truth of that statement. I find that the government propose to pay out about $14,000,000 under this agreement which is before the House to-night. For this money which is to be paid out in subsidies we will receive no direct benefit after it has been paid. If this agreement was entered into primarily to protect the interests of the cattle growers in western Canada as it has been claimed-and I think perhaps there is some ground for that proposition-before the government go ahead and carry out that primary object, the proper thing to do would be to spend this $14,000,000 in completing the Hudson Bay railway and developing the port of Nelson. I am quite certain that within a few short years hundreds of thousands of head of live cattle would be shipped from the northern portion of the prairie provinces to Great Britain via that route.	_
Another thing that would affect the live cattle trade to a considerable extent is the further development of the port of Quebec.
I have brought this matter up in this House on previous occasions and I intend to bring it up again. We find that in western Canada we can deliver our cattle on steamer at Quebec at a saving of from $4 to $5 a head. The facilities for handling cattle there are superior to those at Montreal, and the route is a little shorter over the Transcontinental railway; and I would entreat the government, if they want to assist us in developing our cattle trade, to do something further to develop the port of Quebec. The great difficulty in the way of shipping our cattle through Quebec is this, that owing to, not a discriminatory, but a prohibitive rate on grain over the Transcontinental to the city of Quebec, we are not able to make up mixed cargoes from that port. That is one of the factors in the cattle situation to-day. And while this matter is under discussion, I hope the government will see its way clear at some future time to remove that prohibitive rate and to allow some of our grain to go forward to Quebec so that mixed cargoes may be made up there. The question of government control of rates enters into this resolution. The history of government control of rates in the past has not been such as to encourage us in the 'hope that we are going to receive any material relief from the fact that the government will control rates on these steamships, because the government has absolute control of our railway rates and the government must be responsible for the retention of this prohibitive rate to which I refer.
A consideration of the report before us today, issued by Mr. Preston, reveals that it is noteworthy, not so much for what it says, as for what it fails to say. I have just been comparing it with a former report dealing with steamship rates. I refer to the report of the royal commission appointed two years ago to inquire into grain rates on the Great Lakes. In the report of that royal commission, I find that they went very fully into the earnings of the vessels, the dividends that were paid by the companies and the

values of their vessels. They gave us a great deal of evidence as to what earnings these vessels were making and they gave us further evidence to prove that the values of the vessels were inflated to show reduced earnings, whereas in reality the companies were making much more than their reports would indicate. In the report we are now considering we have not one single iota of evidence to show whether these Atlantic steamships are making enormous profits or whether, as some of the companies claim, they are really going behind. That proves the necessity of referring all this to a special committee of this House with power to bring witnesses here in order that we may obtain all possible information before we go any further.
When we come to consider rates on grain from Montreal to Liverpool, we find that there is no very great rise in those rates in comparison with pre-war figures. I have taken four different years before the war and four years after the war. I find that the cost per bushel of transhipping our grain from Montreal to Liverpool was as follows:

It is rather remarkable that our grain was transported in 1922 at the exact cost at which it was transported in 1913, notwithstanding the fact that coal, wages and overhead costs of ships had increased tremendously during that period. This may be due to the fact that one-half or more than one-half of our grain is handled by tramp steamships over which the combine has had no control.
Mr. Preston, in his report, states that in dealing with this we are faced with adopting one of two alternatives, that is, government ownership or subsidizing private lines. I have no hesitation in saying that, if we must choose between these two, in heaven's name give us government ownership rather than the continuance of a policy of granting subsidies to private concerns. We have government control of rates. We have government control of railway rates, but that has not prevented some of the most iniquitous discrimination from creeping into our rate schedules. W e have indirect government control of rates on the Great Lakes, of the steamship companies, but that has not prs-

vented those companies from fleecing us out of eight or ten million dollars a year in excess rates. I find that the government propose to pay out a subsidy of $1,375,000 a year or, in the ten years under this agreement, we would have paid out $13,750,900. I find that an annual subsidy of $1,375,000 would pay interest on a capital investment of $27,500,000. I would suggest to the government that rather than continue to pay out this subsidy with nothing to show for it at the end, we should increase the capitalization of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, if more ships are necessary, to the extent of $27,500,000. In that way I believe we would accomplish more than we shall by the plan laid before the House by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Last session we discussed at considerable length the question of trade with the West Indies. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) very ably and eloquently placed some illuminating facts before the House in connection with trade with the West Indies, and made some concrete suggestions for the further development of that trade. On that occasion the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) suggested that probably the best course to follow would be for the government to construct two ships, Specially built and equipped for carrying perishable products through tropical regions. That statement of the minister was applauded from every section of this House, I do not believe there was a dissentient voice; and that should be a clear indication to the government that parliament would prefer that policy to a continuation of a subsidy. But when I suggest a further increase of government ownership, I make that suggestion on the understanding that the government will see to it that its merchant marine in future remains out of this combine. About two years ago we had evidence produced before the special committee on Agriculture showing that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine had its feet under the conference table; that it was participating in these regular meetings for rate fixing and that, in fact, in some instances it was the principal sinner. The government must bear some responsibility for that. After nearly two years we recently had an announcement that the government merchant marine had withdrawn from this conference. Yet this same government comes forward to-day and in righteous indignation proceeds to deal with the North Atlantic Steamship Combine. In view of the fact that these prohibitory rates are maintained to prevent us from using the

Transcontinental railway for the transportation of our grain, forcing us at the head of the lakes to deliver that grain to the lake steamships whether we like it or not, and in view of the history of the Canadian merchant marine's connection with the combine, we may be pardoned for doubting to some extent the sincerity of the government. I would earnestly entreat the government to go further into the matter and give us some definite assurance that the Canadian merchant marine will in future keep strictly clear of the combine. I have here an editorial from the Manitoba Free Press in which there is discussed at considerable length the case of a shipment of cattle from Montreal to Dundee by a Colonel Mullins, a cattle shipper.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), discussing this subject a few evenings ago, said that the time had come for us to line up either for or against the combine. The implication of that statement was that any of us who questioned the present proposal and demanded further light on it -were lining up with the combine. I must repudiate that suggestion; we in this section of the House are as anxious as are hon. gentlemen opposite to have the combine dealt with. We want a little more information, however, and in general I believe that most hon. gentlemen in this section of the House would prefer to see some more money spent on the Canadian merchant marine. We should like to see the merchant marine develop so that any money spent upon it would yield us something in return. I would urge the government to turn the whole question over to a special committee, before whom those especially interested
can appear and give testimony, so that we may have the fullest and freest discussion. We should be able to secure every possible information that would assist us in coming to an intelligent understanding on the subject. To refuse to do this, to force the agreement through the House without affording us an ample opportunity to acquire this information, is to suiTOund the whole thing with mystery and suspicion. I hope therefore that before this matter comes to a vote the government will clear up the situation by making some pronouncement of policy along this line.

Mr. Speaker, I make no apology
for prolonging the debate on this subject, as I look upon the action of the government in grappling with ocean freight rates as being as important and far-reaching as an3^ legislation that will come before this parliament. Every citizen in Canada, manufacturer, farmer or labourer, will be beneficially affected by the decrease in transportation charges, whether on land or sea. In dealing with the report I wish to eliminate Mr. Preston entirely, as he is only the instrument used, or the spade that dug up the facts.
The report deals with the problem as to whether there is a combine, conference or sitting-in of certain large shipping interests to consider and make or maintain freight and passenger rates; and I am satisfied that in this particular the case has been established. But if not, I have my own personal experience to draw from. I have before me both the report and the reply of the steamship lines, copies of which have been placed in the hands of some of us. While the reply is not signed, there appears in it some of the names of large shipping companies that operate on the north Atlantic. I do not see anywhere in the document the name of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I find that the steamship companies in this reply take exception to what Mr. Preston states on page 3. I would quote the following from their reply:
As mentioned previously in this report there is no " combine " (which in the present day acceptation of the term implies a monopoly), but merely an association of the regular lines, constituting a very small portion of the carriers on the Atlantic, who have agreed among themselves to quote on various commodities equivalent rates subject to change on notice.
I wonder if that does not mean a combine. I think it establishes very fully, at least it does to my mind, the fact that Mr, Preston was right when he said that there was a conference almost equivalent to a combine.
In April, 1922, the British Admiralty sent a gentleman from England to dispose of the accumulation of war lumber stocks held in

to the Preston report shows, as well as their action in having people around here trying to find out what the attitude of parliament will be. But if we are loyal to Canada and to the people we represent, some action must be taken by this parliament because it is imperative that the lines now operating on the Atlantic reduce their rates, both passenger and freight, so that prosperity may come again to this country, and prosperity can only return in full measure when transportation rates on both water and land are reduced materially from what they are at the present time.
I think some good to Canada will come from submitting this contract to parliament, and I believe that it should go to a special committee for mature consideration. subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: I will admit that the Canadian National Railways, and the whole system of government ownership has bled the Canadian people white; but at the same time I have great confidence in it, and if we would put party bias aside and get down to business management, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine might be in a better position than it is at the present time.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: The hon. member would like to put the steamship line under Sir Henry Thornton, the same gentleman who is in charge of the Canadian National Railways. If under his management the Canadian National system is bleeding the people white, would the hon. member want him also to bleed the people white under the system of a steamship line?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: No. I am not saying anything against the management of the Canadian National because we are gradually getting out of the hole; but I want to say the deficit on the Canadian National cannot continue. If we take into consideration the stock we are buying every year and the equipment, with the deficit, it would amount to nearly a hundred million dollars. I say that this system of going behind cannot continue very long in Canada.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Bankruptcy would result.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
It means bankruptcy if we are going to keep on in this way. With a population of nine million people we cannot pay ten or eleven dollars a head to liquidate the deficit on the Canadian National, and the time will come when we shall be forced into the scheme suggested by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), where we shall have to combine in order to save ourselves.
In closing I say that I intend to vote that this resolution shall go to a committee. I do not know altogether, nor am I satisfied in my own mind, that this is the best scheme. I think there are other schemes which might be suggested, but this is the only scheme that is before us, and we must deal with it upon its merits. When a man speaks ir *w'a House

about a certain matter the people claim, "Oh you are against it" or they say, "You are siding with the steamship lines; you are on the side of the combine". Nothing can be further from my mind. I do not believe in combines. I think they should be fought where we can fight them with any measure of success; but I do not think it is wise to attempt to handle them until we are sure of our ground and have some conception of success in the future. For that reason, I hope, after this matter has been before the committee and all the evidence available is gathered and comes to our hands, that we shall see to it that we cast an intelligent vote either for or against it as the case may be. At the present time I intend to vote that this matter shall go before the committee, and I will await my final decision till the bill comes back from committee.
On motion of Mr. Forke the debate was adjourned.
